summary: This experimental document extends Mobile IPv6 and Proxy Mobile IPv6 fast handovers to support multicast listeners. Fast handover base operations handle unicast, but delay-sensitive multicast applications such as IPTV need support during handover.

eli5.summary: When you move between networks while watching live TV, the stream might stutter. This RFC tries to keep it smooth.

questions: how does multicast work with mobile ipv6
what are mobility option types 60 and 61
what does the m bit in prrtadv mean
subtitle: Lets multicast streams such as IPTV follow a mobile node through fast handovers in Mobile IPv6 and Proxy Mobile IPv6.

tldr.problem: Fast handover protocols speed up unicast traffic when a mobile node moves, but they do not move multicast state, so multicast streams are disrupted.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds two mobility options that carry the node's MLD or IGMP listener state from the previous to the new access router in the existing handover messages, so the new router can join groups and the old one can forward in the meantime.
tldr.outcome: It is an Experimental extension that updates RFC 5568 with an 'M' bit in the Proxy Router Advertisement and registers two new mobility options.

today: RFC 7411 is an Experimental RFC and it updates RFC 5568 by adding the 'M' bit to the Proxy Router Advertisement. No later RFC is listed as obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: The Multicast Handover Gap
sections.content:
Mobile IPv6 (RFC 6275) and Proxy Mobile IPv6 (RFC 5213) cause traffic disruptions on handovers that may be intolerable for gaming or conferencing. Fast handovers for Mobile IPv6 (FMIPv6, RFC 5568) and for Proxy Mobile IPv6 (PFMIPv6, RFC 5949) improve this for unicast only.

Multicast forwarding state is not transferred between access routers by those protocols, so multicast does not get expedited handover. This matters for applications like IPTV, time-critical feeds, conferencing and public safety communication.

The RFC extends both fast handover protocols to carry multicast context for any-source and source-specific multicast. Its design goals are that the context transfer is transparently part of the unicast handover, that neither unicast mobility nor multicast routing is modified, and that mobile nodes in Proxy Mobile IPv6 domains do not take active part. A multicast-unaware node can still do fast handovers with multicast-aware routers.
sections.eli5: The old rules helped phone calls follow you when you move, but not live TV broadcasts. This adds that missing piece.

sections.title: How the Context Transfer Works
sections.content:
The previous access router (PAR, or PMAG in proxy mode) sends the new access router (NAR, or NMAG) the mobile node's multicast groups inside the existing Handover Initiation (HI) message. The NAR answers in its Handover Acknowledgement (HAck), listing the groups it cannot support. The NAR can then join the groups early, and the PAR can add the unicast handover tunnel to its multicast forwarding list so flows travel through the tunnel in parallel with unicast traffic.

The NAR acts as an MLD proxy toward the PAR and stops tunnel forwarding for a group once it receives it natively. Both fast handover protocols have a predictive mode, where the transfer happens before the move, and a reactive mode, where it happens after the node reattaches. In both modes the PAR treats the node's departure or the arrival of the acknowledgment as a multicast LEAVE and prunes as needed.

The aim is a multicast handover performance comparable to unicast handover. Tunnel management is inherited from the unicast protocols, and tunnels stay up until the unicast handover finishes.
sections.eli5: The old network passes a note to the new one listing your favourite channels. The new network starts getting them ready, and the old one sends them across in the meantime.

sections.title: Router and Node Behavior
sections.content:
In FMIPv6, the mobile node itself attaches a Multicast Mobility Option to its Fast Binding Update (FBU). The PAR copies it into HI, takes the Multicast Acknowledgement Option from HAck, and returns it in the Fast Binding Acknowledgement (FBack). If some groups are unsupported, the node can act, for example by home tunneling. A router advertises support with the 'M' bit in the Proxy Router Advertisement.

In PFMIPv6 the node does nothing special. The MAG must send an MLD General Query immediately unless it tracks membership explicitly, builds the option from the listener state, and sends it in HI. In reactive mode the HI/HAck roles are inverted: the NMAG learns the groups with a General Query, joins them and asks the PMAG to forward.

Some rules are firm. The NAR MUST NOT forward more than one flow of the same group to the node. The NAR (NMAG) MUST send a LEAVE to the tunnel when forwarding is no longer needed. The PAR SHOULD forward requested groups but MAY refuse them, for example for load or policy reasons. Multicast packets may still be lost during a handover, and buffering at the PAR can reduce loss at the cost of resources and delay.
sections.eli5: If your phone handles the move itself, it hands over the channel list. If the network handles it, the network just asks who is listening and passes the list along.

sections.title: The New Mobility Options
sections.content:
The RFC defines two mobility options. The Multicast Mobility Option (type 60) carries the listener state, taken from an MLD or IGMP Membership Report with its ICMP header removed. Its option-code says what the payload is: 1 for IGMPv3, 2 for MLDv2, 3 for IGMPv3 from IGMPv2 compatibility mode, and 4 for MLDv2 from MLDv1 compatibility mode.

The Multicast Acknowledgement Option (type 61, option-code 0) carries a status (1 payload type unsupported, 2 requested group service unsupported, 3 administratively prohibited) and the records that could not be transferred.

Because the Length field is 8 bits, an FBU/FBack message pair can carry at most 4 octets of header plus 1024 octets of report payload, which fits not more than 51 minimal Multicast Address Records. A single MLDv2 Report Payload MUST NOT be fragmented, which limits a record to 62 source addresses. Access routers MUST support MLDv2 and IGMPv3, and fall back to the lowest compatibility mode learned.
sections.eli5: There are two kinds of notes: one that says which channels you watch, and one that says which of them the new network cannot supply.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: Transferring context in predictive handovers creates group state at a remote router, possibly without validating the request. A new router may then have to set up complex multicast rerouting and receive large volumes of traffic, so malicious or accidental transfers can burden the backbone and the router itself. The RFC suggests rate control at the access router to limit how often traffic is redirected and the total number of subscriptions. It also notes that the wireless access network is protected from multicast data injection until the requesting node attaches to the new location.
sections.eli5: If anyone could ask a router to start streaming lots of channels, it could be swamped. So the router limits how often and how many it will accept.
